title: Designing for consistency or for availability: what changes
dek: Choosing consistency or availability isn't just a label in your requirements; it changes the architecture. A consistency-first design keeps one source of truth and pays for agreement in latency and in refused requests. An availability-first design lets copies answer on their own and pays in data that can be briefly out of date. Most databases can be set either way.

items: Consistency first: keep one source of truth (one primary database), or coordinate writes across stores (distributed transactions, consensus). Expect higher latency and errors during a split. Typical choices: PostgreSQL or MySQL, Spanner, DynamoDB with strongly consistent reads.

Availability first: serve reads from replicas updated asynchronously, and spread changes with change data capture. Expect stale reads. Typical choices: Cassandra, DynamoDB global tables, Redis replicas.
Many databases are tunable: Cassandra's consistency levels, DynamoDB's ConsistentRead, MongoDB's read and write concerns. The skill is choosing per use case.

One source of truth: keep the data that must be exact in a single primary database. Every write and every read that must be current goes to it. Nothing can disagree because there is only one copy that counts. It limits how far that part scales, but often that part is small: bookings and payments, not menus.

Coordinated writes: when several stores must agree, for example the bookings database and a seat-map cache, coordinate them, with a distributed transaction such as two-phase commit, or by writing through a consensus-based store. Every write now waits for several machines, so latency rises, and during a split the system refuses writes it can't coordinate.

Strongly consistent databases: PostgreSQL and MySQL with reads from the primary; Google Spanner, which keeps strong consistency across regions using synchronised clocks and consensus; DynamoDB with strongly consistent reads (ConsistentRead: true), which read from the partition's leader; and coordination services like etcd or ZooKeeper for small, critical data.

Read replicas with asynchronous replication: any replica can answer reads, even if it is a little behind. Reads scale out and keep working when the primary or a link is down, at the cost of possibly stale data.

Change data capture (CDC): the primary database stays the place where changes are made, and a stream of its changes updates caches, search indexes and other stores in the background. Each of them keeps serving while the updates flow through, a little later.

Databases built for it: Cassandra, which accepts writes on any replica and reconciles later; DynamoDB with eventually consistent reads and global tables across regions; Redis with replicas; and caches and CDNs in general.

body.cap: Consistency first: every write and every exact read goes through one source of truth. Availability first: replicas and caches fed by a change stream answer on their own, a little behind.

body.x: The line between 'consistent' and 'available' databases is blurrier than lists suggest, because many let you choose per request:

items: Cassandra: each read and write names a consistency level. ONE answers from a single replica (fast, available, maybe stale); QUORUM needs a majority, and with QUORUM on both reads and writes a read always sees the latest write; ALL needs every replica.
DynamoDB: reads are eventually consistent by default and half the cost; ConsistentRead gives the latest data from the leader. Global tables replicate across regions asynchronously.
MongoDB: write concern (how many replicas must confirm) and read concern (whether a read may return data that could still be rolled back) are set per operation.
PostgreSQL: reads from the primary are current; reads from asynchronous replicas may lag; synchronous replication makes a commit wait for a replica.

body.cap: With five copies and majority quorums, the side of a split that holds three can keep going; the side with two must refuse, which is consistency chosen per operation.

body.x: Even with a healthy network, waiting for copies to agree costs time. PACELC names that everyday half of the trade-off: if there's a Partition, Availability or Consistency; Else, Latency or Consistency. The concept 'CAP and PACELC in practice' covers it.

items: After choosing consistency or availability, name the building blocks that deliver it: one primary or consensus for consistency; replicas, CDC and caches for availability.
Name a database and its setting, not just its brand: 'DynamoDB with strongly consistent reads for bookings, eventually consistent reads for match pages.'
Say what the user sees during a split: an error, a wait, or slightly old data.
